Question: CaCO3 (s) decomposes by calcination generating CaO (s) and CO2 (g) according to the equation CaCO3 (s) <-> CaO (s) + CO2 (g). In experiment I, a quantity of CaCO3 (s) is placed in a porcelain capsule open to the outside, and in experiment II the same quantity of CaCO3 (s) is placed in a hermetically sealed container. In both experiments the sample was heated to 900 deg C. In which experiment will CaCO3 (s) be able to decompose completely?

Options:
A. In both experiments it will be possible to completely decompose the initial CaCO3 (s)
B. In none of the experiments will it be possible to completely decompose the initial CaCO3 (s)
C. Only in experiment I
D. Only in experiment II

You MUST include the letter(s) of the correct answer (separated by comma if there are many) within the following tags: [ANSWER] and [/ANSWER].
For example, '[ANSWER]<answer>[/ANSWER]', where <answer> is comma- or space-separated list of the correct letters. Always answer in exactly this format of comma-separated letters between the two tags, even if you are unsure. We require this because we use automatic parsing.

Thought: To solve this problem, we need to consider the conditions under which CaCO3 decomposes. The reaction CaCO3 (s) <-> CaO (s) + CO2 (g) is an equilibrium reaction. In an open system, carbon dioxide gas can escape, which shifts the equilibrium towards the products, allowing for the complete decomposition of CaCO3. In a closed system (hermetically sealed container), CO2 cannot escape, and the reaction may reach equilibrium before all the CaCO3 is decomposed. Therefore, only in the open system (Experiment I) is it possible for all the CaCO3 to decompose.
